P1-K1.text: Proposes appending a small set of learned memory tokens that are carried between fixed-size segments, letting a standard transformer read documents far longer than its attention window.

P1-K2.text: Transformers cannot process documents longer than their fixed attention window. "Standard transformers cannot attend beyond a fixed window, which makes long documents impossible to process in a single pass."

P1-K3.text: Learned memory tokens are passed from one segment to the next. "We append a small set of learned memory tokens to every segment and pass their final states to the next segment."

P1-K4.text: Evaluated on a long-document language modeling corpus. "We evaluate on the LongDocs-103 language modeling corpus, whose documents average twelve thousand tokens."

P1-K5.text: Lower perplexity than truncation baselines at equal compute. "Memory tokens reduce perplexity by 1.8 points relative to truncated context at the same compute budget."

P1-K6.text: Memory capacity is fixed and information is lost on very long inputs. "Because the number of memory tokens is fixed, information from early segments is gradually overwritten on very long inputs."

P1-K7.text: Training requires backpropagation through many segments, which is slow. "Training requires backpropagating through many consecutive segments, which makes each update considerably slower than standard training."

P2-K1.text: Replaces softmax attention with a random-feature kernel approximation so attention cost grows linearly with sequence length.

P2-K2.text: Softmax attention is quadratic in sequence length. "The cost of softmax attention grows quadratically with sequence length, which dominates runtime for long inputs."

P2-K3.text: Approximates the softmax kernel with random features to get linear-time attention. "We approximate the softmax kernel with positive random features, which lets attention be computed in time linear in sequence length."

P2-K4.text: Evaluated on LongDocs-103 and a synthetic copy task. "Experiments use LongDocs-103 and a synthetic copy task that requires exact recall of distant tokens."

P2-K5.text: Matches softmax quality on language modeling at a fraction of the cost. "On LongDocs-103 our model matches softmax attention within 0.3 perplexity while running four times faster at length 8192."

P2-K6.text: Approximation error grows on tasks needing exact recall. "We observe that approximation error increases on tasks that require exact recall of individual distant tokens."

P2-K7.text: Random features need to be redrawn during training for stability. "Training is only stable when the random features are periodically redrawn, which adds a tuning burden."

P3-K1.text: Restricts attention to local blocks plus a few global tokens, giving near-linear cost for classifying long documents.

P3-K2.text: Long-document classification is limited by attention cost. "Classifying long documents with transformers is limited by the cost of full attention over thousands of tokens."

P3-K3.text: Combines local block attention with a few global tokens. "Each token attends to its local block and to a small number of global tokens that summarise the whole document."

P3-K4.text: Evaluated on two long-document classification benchmarks. "We report results on the ArXivTopics and LegalLong classification benchmarks."

P3-K5.text: Improves accuracy over truncated baselines. "Block-sparse attention improves accuracy by 3.1 points over truncated baselines on LegalLong."

P3-K6.text: The block size is fixed and must be tuned per dataset. "The block size is fixed in advance and must be tuned separately for every dataset we evaluate."

P4-K1.text: Models sequences with a linear state-space recurrence computed in parallel chunks, extending the memory-token idea to a continuous state.

P4-K2.text: Recurrent memory compresses history poorly. "Discrete memory slots compress the history poorly when the relevant information is spread across the sequence."

P4-K3.text: A linear state-space layer is evaluated chunk by chunk in parallel. "We compute a linear state-space recurrence chunk by chunk, using a parallel scan inside each chunk."

P4-K4.text: Evaluated on LongDocs-103 and a long-range arena style suite. "We evaluate on LongDocs-103 and on a suite of six long-range reasoning tasks."

P4-K5.text: Strong results on long-range reasoning tasks. "Chunked state spaces achieve the best average accuracy on the long-range reasoning suite among linear-time models."

P4-K6.text: State updates do not depend on the input, limiting selective recall. "Because the state transition does not depend on the input, the model cannot selectively ignore irrelevant tokens."

P5-K1.text: Stores past segments in an external index and retrieves the most relevant ones at each step, instead of compressing them into fixed memory.

P5-K2.text: Fixed-size memories forget early evidence needed for question answering. "Fixed-size memories forget early evidence, which is often exactly what a long-context question asks about."

P5-K3.text: Past segments are indexed and retrieved by similarity. "Every processed segment is written to an external index, and the most similar segments are retrieved before answering."

P5-K4.text: Evaluated on long-document QA and on LegalLong. "We evaluate on the NarrativeLong question answering set and reuse the LegalLong documents as a retrieval stress test."

P5-K5.text: Large gains on questions about early parts of documents. "Retrieval improves exact match by 9 points on questions whose answer appears in the first tenth of the document."

P5-K6.text: Retrieval latency grows with document length. "Retrieval latency grows with the number of stored segments, which becomes noticeable for book-length inputs."

P6-K1.text: Re-examines kernelized linear attention and finds that it underperforms softmax attention on retrieval-heavy tasks, then proposes a hybrid that fixes the recall gap.

P6-K2.text: Linear attention is assumed to match softmax quality. "It is widely assumed that kernelized linear attention matches the quality of softmax attention on long inputs."

P6-K3.text: A hybrid layer adds a small exact-attention window to linear attention. "We add a small sliding window of exact softmax attention next to the kernelized linear attention in every layer."

P6-K4.text: Uses the same synthetic copy task and LongDocs-103. "We reuse the synthetic copy task and LongDocs-103 so that our numbers are directly comparable."

P6-K5.text: The hybrid closes most of the recall gap. "The hybrid layer recovers 92 percent of the softmax accuracy on the copy task while keeping linear cost."

P6-K6.text: The hybrid still needs a tuned window size. "The hybrid still requires choosing the window size, and too small a window loses most of the benefit."

P7-K1.text: Makes the state-space transition depend on the current input so the model can choose what to keep, closing the gap with attention on recall tasks.

P7-K2.text: Input-independent state spaces cannot select what to remember. "Input-independent state transitions cannot decide which tokens are worth remembering."

P7-K3.text: State transitions are computed from the current input. "We compute the state transition parameters from the current input token, which makes the recurrence selective."

P7-K4.text: Evaluated on the long-range suite and the copy task. "We evaluate on the six-task long-range suite and on the synthetic copy task."

P7-K5.text: Solves the copy task where earlier linear models fail. "Selective updates solve the synthetic copy task at every length we tested, where earlier linear-time models fail."

P7-K6.text: Hardware-specific kernels are needed for speed. "Reaching the reported speed requires custom fused kernels that are specific to one hardware family."

P8-K1.text: Collects long-context tasks into one benchmark and compares memory, retrieval, attention and state-space models under a shared protocol.

P8-K2.text: Long-context models are evaluated under incompatible protocols. "Long-context models are currently evaluated under incompatible protocols, which makes published numbers hard to compare."

P8-K3.text: A shared protocol with fixed budgets for all model families. "We fix the compute budget and the context length for every model family under one shared protocol."

P8-K4.text: Includes LegalLong, NarrativeLong and the copy task. "The benchmark includes LegalLong, NarrativeLong and the synthetic copy task alongside four new tasks."

P8-K5.text: No single model family wins on every task. "No single model family wins on every task, and retrieval-based models lead on question answering."

P8-K6.text: The benchmark covers English text only. "All tasks in the benchmark are in English, so conclusions may not transfer to other languages."

P4-K7.text: Discrete memory slots compress the history poorly when the relevant information is spread across the sequence. Following the memory-token approach of Moreau and Ibarra, we carry a state across chunks, but make that state continuous. This removes the hard limit on how many slots can be stored.

P6-K7.text: We reuse the synthetic copy task and LongDocs-103 so that our numbers are directly comparable. Contrary to the parity reported by Okoro et al., we find that kernelized attention loses 31 points of accuracy on the copy task. The gap widens as the distance between the copied tokens grows.
